tasks.short: Sell tickets at the gate till, check tickets at the entrance, sort out refunds, and count the till.

steps.what: Visitors buy tickets in the web shop or at a kiosk and scan them at the gate themselves
Attendant sells tickets and collects fees from customers at the gate till
Attendant checks tickets by hand at the entrance
Attendant sorts out refunds and problems with online tickets
Attendant counts the cash drawer and fills in the daily takings: on a paper sheet today; after the change enters the counted cash next to the expected takings the till shows
Attendant checks the takings before closing: counted cash against expected takings per payment type, and a note for any difference
Attendant closes the till with the checked takings for the facility manager

tasks.design: One ticketing system ({OTHER}) serves the web shop, self-service kiosks and the gate till, so many visitors arrive with a ticket and scan it at the gate themselves while the attendant watches the gate and helps. Closing shows expected takings per payment type; the attendant counts the cash, compares, checks and closes the till once.
tasks.previous_blocker: Every ticket was sold and checked at the gate, and takings were counted by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Attraction ticketing systems run web shop, gate till and kiosks on one back end with live reporting.
tasks.still_hard: Families with questions still queue at the till; cash visitors keep the count.
tasks.human_edge: Welcoming a family and solving a ticket problem without a scene.
tasks.altitude: The attendant helps at the gate instead of selling every ticket.

reach.learn: Whether live sales data improve staffing.

evidence.claim: An attraction ticketing system runs web shop, gate till and kiosks on one back end with live reporting; a zoo reports about half its visitors use the kiosks.
Ticket sales touch no high-risk AI area; this design uses no AI.

assumptions: Boundary: from ticket sale to the till counted; pricing is outside.
Input contract: ticket types and prices set by the facility manager in the ticketing system; fallback is the gate till.
Kiosk and web customers' time is outside the attendant's savings.

Refund handling and the check and close of the till keep their full time. s1 keeps 60 and s2 keeps 60 because about 40% of visitors buy online or at a kiosk and scan themselves (s1v, visitor time). s4 keeps 55 because there is less cash to count and the expected totals are worked out by the till, while counting stays.
unknowns: Share of visitors who would buy online or at kiosks.
research_questions: How much shorter are gate queues with self-scan?

incremental.description: Attendant helps visitors at kiosks and scanners.

approvals.approved_version: The day's takings per payment type with the counted cash and any difference note exactly as checked by the attendant in s4c, closed once in the ticketing system for the facility manager; any correction needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: mostly walk-in, cash-paying visitors, so only about 15% buy ahead; s1 and s2 keep 85 and s4 keeps 80 (11.7); high: about 40% buy ahead as assumed (33.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Answer visitors' questions in person, by phone and e-mail, explain ride rules and hand out maps and schedules.

steps.what: Attendant gives visitors information about facilities and entertainment options in person
Attendant answers the same questions by phone and e-mail: types every reply today; after the change takes fewer calls and reads a drafted e-mail reply quoting the FAQ

loop.input: A visitor's e-mail question and the facility's FAQ and house rules.
loop.output: A draft reply quoting the matching FAQ entry or rule with its link.
loop.check: Code checks that the reply body is a verbatim quote of one FAQ or rule entry plus the fixed greeting; questions that match no entry, or mention health, accidents, complaints or refunds, go to the attendant unanswered. The attendant reads the quoted entry against the visitor's question and only uses it if it answers that question; otherwise they write the reply.
loop.stop: One match per e-mail; no match means the attendant writes the reply.
loop.why_not_simpler: Visitors ask in their own words; a keyword filter misses most matches.

steps.what: Attendant checks the final e-mail reply: it answers the question asked, the quoted entry is current, and the visitor's address
Attendant sends the checked reply to the visitor
Attendant explains rules and regulations such as height limits at the ride
Attendant hands out maps and show schedules: to every visitor today; only to those who ask for paper after the change

tasks.design: Opening hours, the day's shows, a map and the house rules sit on the website, entrance screens and the ticket confirmation, so fewer visitors need to ask. E-mail questions get a draft reply quoting the matching FAQ entry, which the attendant reads against the question, checks and sends; health, accidents, complaints and refunds always go to staff, and rules at the ride are explained in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Information lived in leaflets and staff memory; every e-mail was typed.
tasks.enabler_now: Ticketing systems send confirmations with information, and language models can match free-text questions to FAQ entries.
tasks.still_hard: A wrong quoted rule can mislead; the FAQ must be kept current.
tasks.human_edge: Calming a child who is just too short for the ride.
tasks.altitude: The attendant checks drafted replies; rules stay with staff.

reach.task: Keep the FAQ and rules current

evidence.claim: Language models can match free-text questions to a fixed list of answers.
A tribunal held an airline liable for its chatbot's wrong fare advice, so quoted answers must match the source word for word.
A chatbot answering the public must say it is AI; here staff send every reply.

assumptions: Boundary: from a visitor's question to the answer; complaints handling is outside.
Input contract: FAQ, house rules and show schedule kept by the facility manager; fallback is typing replies.
Manager time is outside the attendant's savings.

Rules at the ride are explained in person, and the check and send of each reply keep their full time. s1 keeps 85 because fewer visitors ask; s2 keeps 50 because fewer people phone and e-mail drafts quote the FAQ; s4 keeps 20 for visitors who still want a paper map.
research_questions: Which share of e-mails match an FAQ entry?

already_counted.description: Attendant reads every drafted reply before sending.

incremental.description: Attendant flags questions with no FAQ entry.
Facility manager keeps the FAQ and rules current.

approvals.approved_version: The reply text exactly as checked by the attendant in s2c, sent once by e-mail to the visitor who asked; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few e-mails and visitors who do not read the website, so s1 keeps 95 and s2 keeps 80 (13.8); high: visitors read the information before they come (24.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read shut-down and evacuation procedures, join drills and briefings, confirm reading and learn about changes.

steps.what: Attendant reads the shut-down and emergency procedures in the binder at the ride
Attendant takes part in evacuation drills
Attendant attends the safety briefing at the start of the season
Attendant confirms that procedures were read: signs the paper list today, confirms in the staff app after the change
Attendant asks the supervisor what changed in the procedures

tasks.design: Procedures per ride sit in the staff app ({OTHER}) with the changed parts marked, and the attendant confirms reading there, which replaces the paper list. When a procedure changes, staff assigned to that ride get a message saying what changed; drills and briefings stay in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Procedures were binders at each ride and changes were passed on by word of mouth.
tasks.enabler_now: Staff apps show documents with read confirmations and send messages per group.
tasks.still_hard: Reading is not practice; only drills make evacuation work.
tasks.human_edge: Staying calm and clear with a stuck ride full of scared riders.

reach.task: Show that staff know current procedures
reach.learn: Whether read records with change marks satisfy inspections.

evidence.claim: Staff apps show documents with read confirmations and send messages to groups.
Records per employee that can monitor staff need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from reading procedures to knowing the changes; real emergencies are outside.
Input contract: procedures per ride kept by the safety coordinator with change marks; ride assignments from the shift plan; fallback is the binder.
Read records are for safety, not appraisal.

Drills, briefings and confirming reading keep their full time; the confirmation is the attendant's own record. s1 keeps 60 because changed parts are marked and the attendant need not reread the whole binder. s5 keeps 60 because a message says what changed.
research_questions: Do staff know changed procedures better with change marks?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: procedures and change marks are kept by the safety coordinator.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: procedures change rarely and the coordinator marks changes late, so s1 and s5 keep 85 (4.5); high: changes are marked and messaged as designed (12.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Direct visitors to rides and seats, manage the queue and its waiting time, and seat groups together.

steps.what: Attendant directs patrons to rides, seats and attractions
Attendant guesses and calls out queue waiting times
Attendant seats groups together and fills empty seats

tasks.design: A screen at the queue entrance shows the waiting time worked out from the ride's count of riders per cycle and the queue length, instead of the attendant guessing and calling it out. Directing and seating visitors stay with the attendant.
tasks.previous_blocker: Waiting times were guessed and called out.
tasks.enabler_now: Ride controllers count cycles and riders; a simple formula turns that into waiting time.
tasks.still_hard: Queue length must be measured; breakdowns change the time suddenly.
tasks.human_edge: Keeping a long queue cheerful and fair.

reach.learn: Whether shown waiting times move visitors to shorter queues.

evidence.claim: Waiting time can be computed from riders per cycle and queue length.
Counting riders touches no high-risk AI area.

assumptions: Boundary: from directing visitors to filling the ride; ride operation is outside.
Input contract: rider counts from the ride controller set up by the maintenance team; queue length from a gate counter; fallback is guessing.
Directing and seating do not change.
research_questions: Do visitors spread more evenly with shown waiting times?

incremental.description: Attendant corrects the screen during breakdowns.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: rider counts fail often or the queue has no gate counter, so the attendant still calls out times and s2 keeps 90 (1.7); high: the screen works as designed (5.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The recreation attendant keeps welcoming, guiding and safety; till work, tallies and routine questions shrink.
skills_to_grow: Helping visitors with kiosks and scanners
role.ambitious_version: An attendant who spends the day with visitors instead of behind a till.
